n: Rehoboam goes to Shechem, an ancient center of the northern tribes, where all Israel has gathered to confirm him as king. His acceptance there was not automatic.

f.g: An old covenant site in the hill country of Ephraim, where Joshua renewed Israel’s covenant.

n: Jeroboam, a former official of Solomon who had fled to Egypt after a prophet promised him ten tribes, hears the news and comes back.
The people call Jeroboam to be their spokesman, and together they approach Rehoboam.
Their request is reasonable: Solomon’s taxes and forced labor were crushing. Lighten the load, and we will serve you.

f.g: A wooden bar on oxen — here a picture of heavy taxes and labor.

n: Rehoboam asks for three days to think it over.
First he consults the older advisers who had served Solomon — men of experience.
Their counsel: be kind, serve the people, and speak gently, and they will be loyal forever. Servant leadership wins hearts.

f.w: If thou be kind to this people

n: Rehoboam rejects this wise advice and turns to the young men who had grown up with him in privilege.
He asks his peers how to answer the people’s request for relief.
His friends urge a boastful reply: “My little finger is thicker than my father’s waist” — meaning my weakest effort will be harsher than his strongest.
They suggest he threaten even heavier burdens: Solomon used whips, but Rehoboam will use “scorpions” — possibly barbed whips that stung like scorpions.

f.g: Probably whips with metal barbs or knots, named for their sting.

n: On the third day Jeroboam and the people return as instructed.
Rehoboam speaks harshly, disregarding the elders’ wise counsel.
He repeats the young men’s threats word for word. Pride and inexperience cost him most of his kingdom.

f.g: I will make it even heavier.

n: Behind Rehoboam’s foolishness, God’s purposes were at work. Ahijah had prophesied that ten tribes would be torn from Solomon’s house because of Solomon’s idolatry.

f.g: The turn of events came from God — not excusing Rehoboam, but fulfilling prophecy.

n: The northern tribes reject David’s dynasty with a rallying cry: “We have no share in David — go home, Israel! David, look after your own house.” The united kingdom splits in two.

f.w: What portion have we in David?

f.g: Go home — an old call to disband.

n: Only the Israelites living in Judah’s towns remained under Rehoboam. From now on “Judah” is the southern kingdom and “Israel” usually the northern.
Rehoboam foolishly sent Hadoram, the very official in charge of forced labor, to negotiate. The people stoned him to death, and Rehoboam barely escaped to Jerusalem in his chariot.

f.g: Called Adoram or Adoniram in Kings.

n: The split between north and south continued from then on. The prophets later looked ahead to a day when Judah and Israel would be one again.
